paper_description: This paper presents a transformation technique to convert a complex real-time task system with non-preemptive sections, suspensions, and pipeline dependencies (NPS tasks) into a simpler system with only suspensions. This transformation preserves maximum per-task response times, enabling the application of existing schedulability analysis for suspending tasks to these more complex systems, specifically under the Global Earliest Deadline First (GEDF) scheduling algorithm. The main contribution is a method to bound the tardiness of NPS task systems by leveraging this transformation.

formal_description.statement: Any job T_{h,l,j} in \tau_{NPS} can be NP-blocked for at most c_{h,l} \cdot b_{max} time units.

variables.T_{h,l,j}: the j-th job of subtask T_{h,l}
variables.c_{h,l}: maximum number of computation phases for subtask T_{h,l}
variables.b_{max}: maximum duration of any non-preemptive segment over all subtasks in \tau_{NPS}

assumptions: Job T_{h,l,j} commences executing one of its computation phases.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the total time a job can be non-preemptively blocked.

informal_sketch.intuition: A job can only be non-preemptively blocked when it's trying to start a computation phase. Since each computation phase can be at most b_max long and there are at most c_{h,l} computation phases in total for a job, the total blocking time is bounded by the sum of the maximum lengths of all these non-preemptive sections.
steps: Identify that non-preemptive blocking (NP-blocking) can only occur when a job attempts to start a computation phase.
Recognize that a job has a maximum of c_{h,l} computation phases.
Understand that each computation phase can contain a non-preemptive section of at most b_{max} duration.
Sum the maximum possible blocking time for each computation phase to get the total upper bound on NP-blocking.
key_insights: NP-blocking is tied to the start of computation phases.
The number of computation phases and the maximum non-preemptive section length are the key parameters.

formal_description.statement: For any concrete instantiation \tau_{NPS} of \tau_{NPS}, there exists a concrete instantiation \tau_{PS} of \tau_{PS} such that \tau_{NPS} and \tau_{PS} have equivalent GEDF schedules.

variables.\\tau_{NPS}: the original task system with non-preemptive sections, suspensions, and pipelines
variables.\\tau_{PS}: a transformed task system with only suspensions and pipelines (fully preemptive)
variables.GEDF: Global Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm

assumptions: The task system \tau_{NPS} is a concrete instantiation.
formal_description.conclusion: Demonstrates that a complex NPS task system can be transformed into a simpler suspending-pipeline system while preserving schedule equivalence under GEDF.

informal_sketch.intuition: We can model the negative impact of non-preemptive sections by simply treating their maximum possible blocking time as additional suspension time. This effectively makes the non-preemptive sections preemptible, transforming the system into one that only has suspensions and pipelines.
steps: For each subtask T_{h,l}, increase its suspension time s_{h,l} by c_{h,l} \cdot b_{max}.
This new suspension time accounts for the maximum possible NP-blocking time for any job of T_{h,l}, as established by Lemma 1.
The resulting system \tau_{PS} is equivalent to \tau_{NPS} in terms of GEDF scheduling behavior because any potential NP-blocking in \tau_{NPS} is now explicitly modeled as suspension in \tau_{PS}.
This transformation allows analysis of \tau_{NPS} to be performed on \tau_{PS}.
key_insights: NP-blocking can be conservatively modeled as suspension.
The transformation preserves the relative priority ordering and timing behavior under GEDF.

formal_description.statement: For any subtask T_{h,l}, if the maximum response time of any job of T_{h,l} in any GEDF schedule for \tau_{PS} is z time units, then the maximum response time of any such job in any GEDF schedule for \tau_{NPS} is at most z time units.

variables.T_{h,l}: a subtask in the original NPS task system
variables.\\tau_{PS}: the transformed task system with only suspensions and pipelines
variables.\\tau_{NPS}: the original task system with non-preemptive sections, suspensions, and pipelines

formal_description.conclusion: The maximum response time in the transformed system is an upper bound for the maximum response time in the original system.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since we modeled NP-blocking as additional suspension, the jobs in the transformed system (\tau_{PS}) might experience longer delays (due to the added suspension) compared to the original system (\tau_{NPS}). Therefore, the response time in \tau_{PS} can only be greater than or equal to the response time in \tau_{NPS}. This means any bound found for \tau_{PS} is also a valid bound for \tau_{NPS}.
steps: Recall that Theorem 1 states \tau_{PS} and \tau_{NPS} have equivalent GEDF schedules.
The transformation in Theorem 1 increases suspension times in \tau_{PS} to account for NP-blocking in \tau_{NPS}.
This means that for any job, its execution and suspension in \tau_{PS} is at least as long as its execution and NP-blocking in \tau_{NPS}.
Consequently, the response time in \tau_{PS} is an upper bound for the response time in \tau_{NPS}.
Therefore, if the maximum response time in \tau_{PS} is z, the maximum response time in \tau_{NPS} is at most z.
key_insights: The transformation is conservative: it adds delays (suspensions) that might not always occur in the original system.
This conservativeness ensures that bounds derived for the transformed system are valid for the original system.

formal_description.statement: The total idle blocking time of any job T_{k,i,v} in \tau_{PS} is at most \sum_{j=1}^{k-1} (e_{j,i} + s_{j,i}).

variables.T_{k,i,v}: the v-th job of the k-th stage subtask T_{k,i}
variables.\\tau_{PS}: the transformed task system with only suspensions and pipelines

assumptions: Induction on k (pipeline stage) and v (job index).
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the total idle blocking time for a job in a pipeline task system, which is crucial for transforming pipeline dependencies into suspensions.

informal_sketch.intuition: Idle blocking occurs when a job is ready to execute (or suspend) but cannot because all processors are busy with higher-priority jobs, and there are no lower-priority jobs running non-preemptively to block it. For a pipeline task, a job at stage k can be idle blocked by the unfinished work (execution and suspension) of its upstream predecessors (stages 1 to k-1). The lemma shows that this total idle blocking time is bounded by the sum of the execution and suspension times of all its upstream subtasks.
steps: Define PL-blocking: a job is PL-blocked if its L-predecessor is done, but its U-predecessor is not.
Define idle blocking: a job is idle blocked if it's PL-blocked and at least one processor is idle or running a lower-priority job.
The proof uses induction on the pipeline stage k. The base case (k=1) is trivial as first-stage tasks have no U-predecessor and thus cannot be PL-blocked.
For the inductive step (k > 1), consider two cases based on whether the U-predecessor of the U-predecessor (J_{UU}) is complete.

In both cases, the idle blocking time of T_{k,i,v} is shown to be bounded by the sum of execution and suspension times of its upstream subtasks (T_{1,i} to T_{k-1,i}). This is because any idle time for T_{k,i,v} is effectively caused by the remaining work of its upstream jobs.

The bound is derived by considering the worst-case scenario where upstream jobs complete as late as possible, and the current job is blocked by any remaining execution or suspension time of its upstream predecessors.
key_insights: Idle blocking is a consequence of pipeline dependencies and processor availability.
The total idle blocking time for a job is related to the total work of its upstream pipeline stages.
The proof relies on a careful inductive argument considering the completion times of upstream jobs.

formal_description.statement: If L3.1 and L3.2 hold, then ET(T_{k,i,v+1}) \le max(r_{1,i,v}, F(T_{1,i,v-1})) + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \Delta_j + k \cdot (e_{max_{k-1,i}} + s_{max_{k-1,i}}).

variables.ET(T_{k,i,v+1}): Earliest Enabled Time of job T_{k,i,v+1}
variables.\\Delta_j: total length of preemption intervals for U-jobs of T_{k,i,v+1} or T_{k,i,v} within specific time intervals
variables.e_{max_{k-1,i}}: maximum execution cost among subtasks T_{1,i} to T_{k-1,i}
variables.s_{max_{k-1,i}}: maximum suspension length among subtasks T_{1,i} to T_{k-1,i}

assumptions: L3.1: T_{k-1,i,v} and T_{k-1,i,v+1} are both tardy.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides an upper bound on the earliest time a job in a pipeline can become enabled, considering preemption of its upstream jobs.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma helps determine when a job in a pipeline can start executing. It considers the release time of the first stage, the completion of previous jobs, and the time lost due to preemptions of upstream jobs. The bound is derived by summing up these delays.
steps: The lemma aims to bound the Earliest Enabled Time (ET) of a job T_{k,i,v+1}.
It relies on two conditions (L3.1 and L3.2) related to the tardiness of upstream jobs and the completion of the current job relative to its U-predecessor's successor.
The proof uses induction on the pipeline stage k.
The base case (k=2) establishes the bound based on the completion of the L-predecessor and preemption intervals.
The inductive step (k > 2) builds upon the bound for stage k-1, incorporating the additional preemption intervals and the maximum execution/suspension costs of the upstream stages.
The term \sum_{j=1}^{k} \Delta_j accounts for the total time lost due to preemption of any U-job of T_{k,i,v+1} or T_{k,i,v}.
The term k \cdot (e_{max_{k-1,i}} + s_{max_{k-1,i}}) accounts for the maximum possible execution and suspension time of the upstream stages.
key_insights: Preemption of upstream jobs significantly impacts when a downstream job can become enabled.
The bound is a sum of release/completion times, preemption penalties, and worst-case upstream work.
This lemma is a building block for bounding idle blocking times.

formal_description.statement: The total idle blocking time of any two consecutive jobs T_{k,i,v} and T_{k,i,v+1} in \tau_{PS} is at most k \cdot (e_{max_{k-1,i}} + s_{max_{k-1,i}}).

variables.T_{k,i,v}, T_{k,i,v+1}: two consecutive jobs of the k-th stage subtask T_{k,i}
variables.e_{max_{k-1,i}}: maximum execution cost among subtasks T_{1,i} to T_{k-1,i}
variables.s_{max_{k-1,i}}: maximum suspension length among subtasks T_{1,i} to T_{k-1,i}
variables.\\tau_{PS}: the transformed task system with only suspensions and pipelines

assumptions: Both T_{k,i,v} and T_{k,i,v+1} are idle-blocked.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a tighter upper bound on the total idle blocking time for a pair of consecutive jobs in a pipeline, which is essential for transforming pipeline dependencies into suspensions.

informal_sketch.intuition: This lemma refines the bound on idle blocking time from Lemma 2 by considering two consecutive jobs. It shows that the combined idle blocking time for these two jobs is bounded by the maximum execution and suspension costs of their upstream stages, multiplied by the number of stages. This tighter bound is crucial for the transformation of pipeline tasks into independent suspending tasks.
steps: The lemma aims to bound the sum of idle blocking times for two consecutive jobs, T_{k,i,v} and T_{k,i,v+1}.
It considers the case where both jobs are idle-blocked, implying that their upstream predecessors are tardy and they complete before their respective U-predecessor's successor.
The proof uses induction on the job index v.
The base case (v=2k) handles initial jobs that might not be idle-blocked.
For the inductive step (v > 2k), it leverages Lemma 3 to bound the earliest enabled time of T_{k,i,v+1}.
It then argues that if a job is idle-blocked, it must be because all processors are occupied by higher-priority jobs (which are its U-jobs).
The total idle blocking time is then related to the preemption intervals of these U-jobs (\Delta_j) and the maximum execution/suspension costs of the upstream stages.
The final bound is k \cdot (e_{max_{k-1,i}} + s_{max_{k-1,i}}), which represents the total work of the upstream stages that could cause idle blocking.
key_insights: Considering consecutive jobs provides a tighter bound on idle blocking.
The bound is directly related to the total work of the upstream pipeline stages.
This lemma is critical for converting pipeline blocking into suspension time.

formal_description.statement: For any concrete instantiation \tau_{PS} of \tau_{PS}, there exists a concrete instantiation \tau_{S} of \tau_{S} such that \tau_{PS} and \tau_{S} have equivalent GEDF schedules.

variables.\\tau_{PS}: a task system with only suspensions and pipelines (fully preemptive)
variables.\\tau_{S}: a task system with only suspensions (no pipelines, fully preemptive)
variables.GEDF: Global Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm

assumptions: The task system \tau_{PS} is a concrete instantiation.
formal_description.conclusion: Demonstrates that a suspending-pipeline task system can be transformed into a simpler suspending-only task system while preserving schedule equivalence under GEDF.

informal_sketch.intuition: Pipeline dependencies (PL-blocking) can be converted into additional suspension times for each stage. By treating the maximum possible idle blocking time (as bounded by Lemma 4) as suspension time for each subtask, we can effectively eliminate the pipeline structure and create independent suspending tasks.
steps: For each subtask T_{h,l} (where h > 1) in \tau_{PS}, transform it into an independent suspending task.
The original execution time e_{h,l} remains the same.
The suspension time s_{h,l} is increased by an amount that accounts for the maximum possible idle blocking time of T_{h,l}.
According to Lemma 4, this added suspension time is bounded by k \cdot (e_{max_{k-1,i}} + s_{max_{k-1,i}}), where k is the stage number.
This transformation effectively removes the precedence constraints between pipeline stages, as the potential delays are now modeled as suspensions within each stage.
The resulting system \tau_{S} consists of independent suspending tasks, each corresponding to a subtask of the original pipeline task.
key_insights: Pipeline blocking (PL-blocking) can be modeled as suspension.
Lemma 4 provides the necessary bound for this added suspension time.
Each stage of a pipeline task becomes an independent suspending task in \tau_{S}.

formal_description.statement: For any subtask T_{h,l}, if the maximum response time of any job of T_{h,l} in any GEDF schedule for \tau_{S} is z time units, then the maximum response time of any such job in any GEDF schedule for \tau_{PS} is at most z time units.

variables.T_{h,l}: a subtask in the pipeline task system \tau_{PS}
variables.\\tau_{S}: the transformed task system with only suspensions
variables.\\tau_{PS}: the task system with only suspensions and pipelines

formal_description.conclusion: The maximum response time in the transformed suspending-only system is an upper bound for the maximum response time in the original suspending-pipeline system.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to Corollary 1, this corollary states that the transformation from \tau_{PS} to \tau_{S} is conservative. By adding suspension times to model pipeline blocking, the response times in \tau_{S} can only be greater than or equal to those in \tau_{PS}. Thus, any bound derived for \tau_{S} is also a valid bound for \tau_{PS}.
steps: Theorem 2 establishes that \tau_{S} and \tau_{PS} have equivalent GEDF schedules.
The transformation in Theorem 2 increases suspension times in \tau_{S} to account for pipeline blocking (idle blocking) in \tau_{PS}.
This means that for any job, its execution and suspension in \tau_{S} is at least as long as its execution and potential pipeline blocking in \tau_{PS}.
Consequently, the response time in \tau_{S} is an upper bound for the response time in \tau_{PS}.
Therefore, if the maximum response time in \tau_{S} is z, the maximum response time in \tau_{PS} is at most z.
key_insights: The transformation from pipeline to independent suspending tasks is conservative.
Added suspension times ensure that bounds derived for the simpler system are valid for the more complex one.

formal_description.statement: The tardiness of any task T_l in \tau_S scheduled under GEDF is at most x + e_l + s_l, where x \ge V \cdot \frac{1}{(1-\xi_{max})} \cdot m - U_{sum} - U_{cL}, provided U_{sum} + U_{cL} < (1-\xi_{max}) \cdot m. V = E_{sum} + E_{cL} + u_{s,max} \cdot S_{sum} + (m - 1)e_l + m \cdot s_l + 3n \cdot s_{max}.

variables.T_l: a task in \tau_S (a suspending task system)
variables.\\tau_S: a periodic task system with only suspensions
variables.GEDF: Global Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm
variables.x: a value derived from system parameters
variables.\\xi_{max}: maximum suspension ratio of any task
variables.U_{cL}: sum of the min(m-1, c) largest computational task utilizations
variables.V: a complex expression involving system parameters
variables.E_{sum}: total execution cost of all suspending tasks
variables.E_{cL}: sum of the min(m-1, c) largest computational task execution costs
variables.u_{s,max}: maximum utilization of any suspending task
variables.S_{sum}: total suspension length of all tasks
variables.s_{max}: maximum suspension length of any task

assumptions: Task system \tau_S consists only of suspending tasks.
Utilization condition U_{sum} + U_{cL} < (1-\xi_{max}) \cdot m holds.
formal_description.conclusion: Provides a bound on the maximum tardiness for any task in a suspending-only task system under GEDF, given certain utilization constraints.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem, from prior work [9], provides a way to calculate the maximum lateness (tardiness) of any job in a system where tasks can only suspend. It's a complex formula that accounts for total system load, individual task characteristics, and the number of processors. The key idea is that if the system is not too overloaded (satisfying the utilization condition), the tardiness can be bounded.
steps: The theorem is based on analyzing the worst-case scenario for tardiness in a suspending task system under GEDF.

It considers various factors contributing to tardiness: total execution and suspension times (E_{sum}, S_{sum}), the load from high-utilization computational tasks (U_{cL}, E_{cL}), the maximum utilization of any single suspending task (u_{s,max}), and the maximum suspension ratio (\xi_{max}).
The parameter 'x' is a calculated value that represents a bound on the 'extra' delay a job might experience beyond its own execution and suspension.
The formula for 'x' involves a complex combination of these system parameters, aiming to capture the worst-case interference and load.
The condition U_{sum} + U_{cL} < (1-\xi_{max}) \cdot m is a crucial schedulability condition. If this is not met, tardiness can grow unboundedly.
The final tardiness bound is x + e_l + s_l, meaning the maximum tardiness is the calculated 'extra' delay plus the task's own worst-case execution and suspension time.
key_insights: Tardiness bounds are achievable in suspending systems if utilization is managed.
The bound is a function of global system load and individual task parameters.
The utilization condition is critical for bounded tardiness.

formal_description.statement: The tardiness of any task T_l in \tau_S (and thus \tau_{NPS}) scheduled under GEDF is at most x+e_l +s_l, where x is defined in Eq. (1), provided U_{sum} + U_{cL} < (1-\xi_{max})\cdot m.

variables.T_l: a task in \tau_{NPS} (or its transformed equivalent in \tau_S)
variables.\\tau_{NPS}: the original task system with non-preemptive sections, suspensions, and pipelines
variables.\\tau_{S}: the transformed task system with only suspensions
variables.GEDF: Global Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm
variables.x: a value derived from system parameters (same as in Theorem 3)
variables.U_{cL}: sum of the min(m-1, c) largest computational task utilizations
variables.\\xi_{max}: maximum suspension ratio of any task

assumptions: The NPS task system \tau_{NPS} has been transformed into \tau_S.
Utilization condition U_{sum} + U_{cL} < (1-\xi_{max}) \cdot m holds.
formal_description.conclusion: Extends the tardiness bound from suspending-only systems (Theorem 3) to NPS task systems by leveraging the transformations presented in the paper.

informal_sketch.intuition: This theorem is the main result of the paper. It states that by transforming a complex NPS task system into a simpler suspending-only system (\tau_S), we can apply the existing tardiness bound (Theorem 3) to the transformed system. Since the transformations preserve response time bounds (Corollaries 1 and 2), the tardiness bound derived for \tau_S is also valid for the original NPS system.
steps: The paper's core contribution is the transformation of an NPS task system (\tau_{NPS}) into a suspending-only system (\tau_S) through two stages: \tau_{NPS} \rightarrow \tau_{PS} \rightarrow \tau_S.

Theorem 1 and Corollary 1 show that the transformation from \tau_{NPS} to \tau_{PS} (handling non-preemptive sections) preserves response time bounds, meaning max response time in \tau_{PS} \ge max response time in \tau_{NPS}.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 2 show that the transformation from \tau_{PS} to \tau_S (handling pipelines) also preserves response time bounds, meaning max response time in \tau_S \ge max response time in \tau_{PS}.
Combining these, the maximum response time in \tau_S is an upper bound for the maximum response time in \tau_{NPS}.
Therefore, any tardiness bound derived for \tau_S using Theorem 3 can be applied to \tau_{NPS}.

The theorem states that the tardiness of any task T_l in \tau_{NPS} is at most x + e_l + s_l, where x is calculated using the same formula as in Theorem 3, provided the overall utilization condition holds.
key_insights: The paper's transformations are key to applying existing analysis to complex systems.
The conservativeness of the transformations ensures that derived bounds are valid.
The final tardiness bound is directly inherited from the analysis of suspending-only systems.
